concepts: Continuity of piecewise functions involving the greatest integer function
questions.question: Let a function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined as $f(x)=\begin{cases}\sin x-e^{x}, & \text{if } x\le0\\ a+[-x], & \text{if } 0<x<1\\ 2x-b, & \text{if } x\ge1\end{cases}$ where $[x]$ is the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$. If $f$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$, then $(a+b)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: On $(0,1)$ the integer part $[-x]$ is the constant $-1$, so only the two joints $x=0$ and $x=1$ need checking.
solution: For $0<x<1$ we have $-1<-x<0$, so $[-x]=-1$ and $f(x)=a-1$. Hence $\text{RHL}=a-1$.
Continuity at $x=1$: $\text{LHL}=a-1$ (the middle piece is the constant $a-1$) and $f(1)=2-b=\text{RHL}$.
useful_results: For $x\in(0,1)$: $[x]=0$, $[-x]=-1$, $[2x]=0$ or $1$ according as $x<\frac12$ or $x\ge\frac12$; recognise these constants at once.
A piecewise function is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$ iff it is continuous at each joint (each piece here is continuous on its own interval): one equation per joint, so two joints fix two unknowns.
$[-x]=-[x]-1$ when $x\notin\mathbb{Z}$ and $[-x]=-[x]$ when $x\in\mathbb{Z}$.

concepts: Continuity at a point
Standard limits: logarithmic and trigonometric expansions
questions.question: Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined as $f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x^{3}}{(1-\cos2x)^{2}}\,\log_e\left(\dfrac{1+2xe^{-2x}}{(1-xe^{-x})^{2}}\right), & x\ne0\\ \alpha, & x=0\end{cases}$. If $f$ is continuous at $x=0$, then $\alpha$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Split the logarithm and use $\frac{\ln(1+t)}{t}\to1$ so that each part contributes $2xe^{-2x}$ or $2xe^{-x}$.
solution: Using $\lim_{t\to0}\frac{\ln(1+t)}{t}=1$ the bracket equals $2he^{-2h}+2he^{-h}$ up to factors tending to $1$ (both $2he^{-2h}\to0$ and $-he^{-h}\to0$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Replace every factor by its leading-order (Taylor) form: only the first-order term of $\ln(\cdot)$ and $\sin h\sim h$ matter.

useful_results: Leading-order rule: if $u\to0$ then $\ln(1+u)\sim u$, $\sin u\sim u$, $1-\cos u\sim\frac{u^2}{2}$, $\tan u\sim u$, $e^u-1\sim u$ - only the product/quotient of the leading terms matters, provided no cancellation occurs.
$1-\cos2x=2\sin^2x\Rightarrow(1-\cos2x)^2=4\sin^4x\sim4x^4$.
For a function defined by a limit at one point, continuity just means the defined value equals that limit.

concepts: Continuity at a point
Greatest integer function and one-sided limits
questions.question: Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined as $f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\lambda|x^2-5x+6|}{\mu(5x-x^2-6)}, & x<2\\ e^{\frac{\tan(x-2)}{x-[x]}}, & x>2\\ \mu, & x=2\end{cases}$ where $[x]$ is the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$. If $f$ is continuous at $x=2$, then $\lambda+\mu$ is:
questions.key_idea: Left of $2$ the quotient is the constant $-\lambda/\mu$, and right of $2$ we have $[x]=2$, so the exponent is $\frac{\tan h}{h}\to1$.
solution: For $x\to2^+$: $[x]=2$, so $x-[x]=x-2=h\to0^+$ and the exponent is $\frac{\tan h}{h}\to1$. Hence $f(2^+)=e^1=e$.
useful_results: If $(x-a)(x-b)>0$ on one side of a root, then $\frac{|P(x)|}{P(x)}=\pm1$ there: the absolute value just fixes a constant sign.
Right of an integer $n$: $[x]=n$, so $x-[x]=x-n\to0^+$; left of $n$: $x-[x]\to1^-$.
$\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\tan h}{h}=1$ and $\lim_{u\to c}e^{u}=e^{c}$, so an exponent with a finite limit passes through $e^{(\cdot)}$.

concepts: Continuity at a point
Standard limits: $1^\infty$ form and trigonometric ratios
questions.question: Let $f:\left(-\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined as $f(x)=\begin{cases}(1+|\sin x|)^{\frac{3a}{|\sin x|}}, & -\frac{\pi}{4}<x<0\\ b, & x=0\\ e^{\cot4x/\cot2x}, & 0<x<\frac{\pi}{4}\end{cases}$. If $f$ is continuous at $x=0$, then the value of $6a+b^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Both sides are exponentials: the left one is a $1^\infty$ form giving $e^{3a}$, the right one has exponent $\frac{\tan2x}{\tan4x}\to\frac12$.
solution: Continuity at $0$ requires $f(0^-)=f(0)=f(0^+)$, i.e. $b=\lim_{x\to0^-}(1+|\sin x|)^{\frac{3a}{|\sin x|}}=\lim_{x\to0^+}e^{\cot4x/\cot2x}$.
Left side: $\lim(1+|\sin x|)^{3a/|\sin x|}=e^{\lim 3a\cdot\frac{|\sin x|}{|\sin x|}}=e^{3a}$, since $(1+t)^{1/t}\to e$ with $t=|\sin x|\to0$.
Right side: $\frac{\cot4x}{\cot2x}=\frac{\tan2x}{\tan4x}\to\frac{2x}{4x}=\frac12$, so the limit is $e^{1/2}$.
Therefore $b=e^{3a}=e^{1/2}$, which gives $3a=\frac12$, i.e. $a=\frac16$, and $b=\sqrt e$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF names the sides the wrong way round: it takes the $(1+|\sin x|)^{3a/|\sin x|}$ branch as $x\to0^+$ and the $e^{\cot4x/\cot2x}$ branch as $x\to0^-$, whereas the first piece is defined for $x<0$ and the second for $x>0$. It also jumps to $\frac{\tan2x}{\tan4x}$ without stating its limit $\frac12$. Both fixed; $a=\frac16$, $b=\sqrt e$ and the answer are unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Evaluate $\frac{\tan2x}{\tan4x}$ with the double-angle identity instead of the standard limit.
solution: As $x\to0^+$, $\tan2x\to0$, so the ratio tends to $\frac12$ and $f(0^+)=e^{1/2}$.
Take natural logs on the left piece: $\ln f=\frac{3a\ln(1+|\sin x|)}{|\sin x|}\to3a$ because $\frac{\ln(1+t)}{t}\to1$.

useful_results: $1^\infty$ rule: $\lim(1+u)^{v}=e^{\lim uv}$ when $u\to0$, $v\to\infty$.
$\cot A/\cot B=\tan B/\tan A$, and $\frac{\tan kx}{\tan mx}\to\frac km$ as $x\to0$.
$\lim_{t\to0}(1+t)^{c/t}=e^{c}$: here $t=|\sin x|$ and $c=3a$.

concepts: Continuity and differentiability of a function defined through a maximum (running maximum)
questions.question: Let $f:[0,\infty)\to[0,3]$ be a function defined by $f(x)=\begin{cases}\max\{\sin t:0\le t\le x\}, & 0\le x\le\pi\\ 2+\cos x, & x>\pi\end{cases}$. Then which of the following is true:
options: $f$ is not continuous exactly at two points in $(0,\infty)$
$f$ is continuous everywhere but not differentiable exactly at one point in $(0,\infty)$
$f$ is continuous everywhere but not differentiable exactly at two points in $(0,\infty)$
questions.key_idea: The running maximum of $\sin t$ equals $\sin x$ up to $\frac\pi2$, then stays $1$; the joints $\frac\pi2$ and $\pi$ have matching values and slopes.
solution: For $0\le x\le\frac\pi2$ the maximum of $\sin t$ on $[0,x]$ is $\sin x$ (increasing). For $\frac\pi2\le x\le\pi$ it is $1$.
So $f(x)=\sin x$ for $0\le x<\frac\pi2$; $f(x)=1$ for $\frac\pi2\le x\le\pi$; $f(x)=2+\cos x$ for $x>\pi$.
Hence $f$ is differentiable everywhere in $(0,\infty)$, option (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Write the first branch as the composite $f(x)=\sin\left(\min\left(x,\frac\pi2\right)\right)$; the kink of $\min$ is killed by $\cos\frac\pi2=0$.
solution: For $0\le x\le\pi$, $\max_{0\le t\le x}\sin t=\sin(\min(x,\frac\pi2))$ because $\sin$ increases on $[0,\frac\pi2]$ and its maximum value is $1$ at $\frac\pi2$.
The only non-smooth point of $\min(x,\frac\pi2)$ is $x=\frac\pi2$, where the slope drops from $1$ to $0$.
By the chain rule the one-sided derivatives of $f$ at $\frac\pi2$ are $\cos\frac\pi2\cdot1=0$ and $\cos\frac\pi2\cdot0=0$: equal, so $f$ is differentiable there.
At $x=\pi$: $f(\pi)=1$ and both $2+\cos x$ and the constant $1$ equal $1$; slopes $-\sin\pi=0$ and $0$ agree.
So $f$ is differentiable on all of $(0,\infty)$ - option (B), same answer.

useful_results: The running maximum $M(x)=\max_{t\le x}\varphi(t)$ is non-decreasing and continuous when $\varphi$ is continuous; it follows $\varphi$ until $\varphi$ first stops rising, then it is constant. At a local maximum of $\varphi$ ($\varphi'=0$) the two parts join smoothly.
A joint is differentiable iff the one-sided limits of the derivatives agree and the function is continuous there (for differentiable pieces).
$\max(f,g)=\frac{f+g+|f-g|}{2}$, $\min(f,g)=\frac{f+g-|f-g|}{2}$: corners occur only where $f=g$ and $f'\ne g'$.

concepts: Differentiability of a function defined through a maximum (running maximum)
questions.question: Let a function $g:[0,4]\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined as $g(x)=\begin{cases}\max\{t^3-6t^2+9t-3\},\ 0\le t\le x, & 0\le x\le3\\ 4-x, & 3<x\le4\end{cases}$, then the number of points in the interval $(0,4)$ where $g(x)$ is NOT differentiable, is ______.
questions.key_idea: The running maximum of the cubic follows it up to its local maximum at $t=1$, then stays flat at $1$; only the joint with $4-x$ at $x=3$ has unequal slopes.
solution: $y(1)=1$ is a local maximum and $y(3)=-3$ a local minimum; also $y(0)=-3$, so $y$ rises on $[0,1]$ and the maximum over $[0,x]$ stays $1$ for $1\le x\le3$.
Hence $g$ is not differentiable at exactly one point ($x=3$). Answer: $1$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF lists $g'(x)=4$ for $3<x\le4$; the derivative of $4-x$ is $-1$. Its conclusion ($g'(3^-)\ne g'(3^+)$, one point) is unchanged. Also the PDF's range label '$0\le n\le1$' is a typo for $0\le x\le1$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Running-maximum geometry: $g$ leaves the cubic exactly at its peak, where the tangent is horizontal, so no kink; the kink can only appear where the flat part meets $4-x$.
solution: The maximum over $[0,x]$ of a continuous function changes from 'tracking the function' to 'constant' at a point where the function reaches a local maximum, i.e. at $t=1$ where the slope is $0$ - the same as the slope $0$ of the constant, so there is no corner at $x=1$.
The constant stage $g=1$ runs while $y(t)\le1$ for $t\le3$ (since $y(3)=-3$ and the cubic never exceeds $1$ on $[1,3]$): it ends at $x=3$ because the definition switches to $4-x$.
Value check: $4-3=1$, so $g$ is continuous at $3$; the slopes $0$ and $-1$ differ, so $x=3$ is a corner.
Exactly one corner in $(0,4)$: answer $1$ (same answer).

useful_results: If $M(x)=\max_{0\le t\le x}\varphi(t)$, then $M$ is non-decreasing, and $M'(x)=\varphi'(x)$ where $M=\varphi$, $0$ where it is constant: joins at a local maximum of $\varphi$ are always smooth.
Critical points of $t^3-6t^2+9t-3$: $t=1,3$ (cubic $t^3-6t^2+9t=t(t-3)^2$ shifted); the local maximum value is $1$.
At a joint where the function is continuous, compare the derivatives of the two pieces; differing one-sided derivatives mean a corner.

concepts: Continuity and differentiability of a function and its shifts (corners of a combination)
questions.question: Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a function defined as $f(x)=\begin{cases}3\left(1-\dfrac{|x|}{2}\right), & \text{if } |x|\le2\\ 0, & \text{if } |x|>2\end{cases}$. Let $g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be given by $g(x)=f(x+2)-f(x-2)$. If $n$ and $m$ denote the number of points in $\mathbb{R}$ where $g$ is not continuous and not differentiable, respectively, then $n+m$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: $f$ is a continuous 'tent', so $g$ is continuous everywhere; the corners of the two shifted tents are $-4,-2,0$ and $0,2,4$, and the corner at $0$ cancels.
solution: All pieces agree at the joints: $g(-4)=0$, $g(-2)=3$, $g(2)=-3$, $g(4)=0$. So $g$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$ and $n=0$.
The graph is a zig-zag with corners at $(-4,0)$, $(-2,3)$, $(2,-3)$, $(4,0)$. At $x=0$ both sides have slope $-\frac32$, so $g$ is smooth there.

alternate_solutions.idea: Count corners by slope jumps: a tent contributes a slope change at each of its three corners; the slope jumps of $f(x+2)$ and $-f(x-2)$ add up, and any total jump of $0$ means no corner.
solution: The slope of $f$ is $0$ for $x<-2$, $+\frac32$ on $(-2,0)$, $-\frac32$ on $(0,2)$, $0$ for $x>2$. So its slope jumps are $+\frac32$ at $-2$, $-3$ at $0$, $+\frac32$ at $2$.
$f(x+2)$ has these jumps at $-4,-2,0$; $-f(x-2)$ has the negatives $-\frac32,+3,-\frac32$ at $0,2,4$.
The jump at $0$ cancels, leaving corners at $-4,-2,2,4$: $m=4$; $g$ is a sum of continuous functions, so $n=0$.

useful_results: A sum of continuous functions is continuous; for corners, add the slope jumps - a corner survives only when the total jump is non-zero.
The tent $3\left(1-\frac{|x|}{2}\right)^{+}$ has corners at $-2,0,2$; shifts move the corner points by $\mp2$.
$f(x+a)$ shifts the graph left by $a$; $f(x-a)$ shifts it right by $a$.

concepts: Continuity at a point and limit of a ratio
Polynomial with given conditions
questions.question: Consider the function $f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{P(x)}{\sin(x-2)}, & x\ne2\\ 7, & x=2\end{cases}$ where $P(x)$ is a polynomial such that $P''(x)$ is always a constant and $P(3)=9$. If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=2$, then $P(5)$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Since $\sin(x-2)\to0$, continuity forces $P(2)=0$, and then $\frac{P(x)}{x-2}\to7$ pins down the linear factor.
solution: $P''(x)$ is a constant, so $P$ is a polynomial of degree at most $2$.
The denominator $\to0$, so the numerator must also tend to $0$: $P(2)=0$ and $P(x)=(x-2)(ax+b)$. (The linear case is covered by $a=0$.)

alternate_solutions.idea: Taylor-expand $P$ about the point $x=2$: continuity gives $P(2)=0$ and $P'(2)=7$, and the constant second derivative leaves only one unknown.
solution: $\frac{P(x)}{\sin(x-2)}\to7$ with $\sin(x-2)\sim(x-2)$ forces $P(2)=0$ and $P'(2)=7$ (the derivative of $P$ at $2$ is the limit of the ratio).

useful_results: If $\frac{N(x)}{D(x)}\to L$ finite with $D(a)=0$, then $N(a)=0$; and if $D'(a)\ne0$ then $N'(a)=L\,D'(a)$. Here $D=\sin(x-2)$ and $D'(2)=1$.
A polynomial with $P''$ constant has degree $\le2$: $P(x)=P(a)+P'(a)(x-a)+\frac{P''}{2}(x-a)^2$.
Continuity of a quotient at a root of the denominator is a statement about $P(a)=0$ and $P'(a)$.

concepts: Continuity and differentiability of functions with the greatest integer function
Fractional part of $x$
questions.question: Let $f:[0,3]\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined by $f(x)=\min\{x-[x],\,1+[x]-x\}$ where $[x]$ is the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$. Let $P$ denote the set containing all $x\in[0,3]$ where $f$ is discontinuous, and $Q$ denote the set containing all $x\in(0,3)$ where $f$ is not differentiable. Then the sum of the number of elements in $P$ and $Q$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: $x-[x]=\{x\}$ and $1+[x]-x=1-\{x\}$, so $f$ is a continuous zig-zag with corners at the integers and at the half-integers.
solution: Graph: on each $[n,n+1)$ it rises with slope $1$ from $0$ to $\frac12$ at $n+\frac12$ and then falls with slope $-1$ towards $0$ at $n+1$; at each integer the value is $0$, matching both sides.
Non-differentiable points in $(0,3)$: the valleys at $x=1,2$ and the peaks at $x=\frac12,\frac32,\frac52$ (slope changes between $\pm1$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Recognise $f(x)$ as the distance from $x$ to the nearest integer, $d(x)=\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb{Z})$.
solution: For $x\in[n,n+1)$ the distance to the nearest integer is $\min(x-n,\,n+1-x)=\min(\{x\},1-\{x\})$, so $f(x)=\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb{Z})$.
A distance function is continuous (it is $1$-Lipschitz), so $f$ has no discontinuity and $n(P)=0$.
$\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb{Z})=|x-n|$ near an integer $n$ (corner at $n$), and the nearest integer switches at the midpoint $n+\frac12$ where the graph has a peak (another corner).
In $(0,3)$ the corners are at $1,2$ and $\frac12,\frac32,\frac52$: five points.

useful_results: $\min(\{x\},1-\{x\})=\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb{Z})$ is continuous, periodic with period $1$, with corners at all multiples of $\frac12$ (peaks at the half-integers, zeros at the integers).
$\max(\{x\},1-\{x\})=1-\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb{Z})$ is the same zig-zag flipped.
A zig-zag between the endpoints $0$ and $3$ has corners at every integer and half-integer strictly inside, here $2+3=5$.

concepts: Continuity and differentiability of functions with the greatest integer function
Minimum of two functions
questions.question: Let $[t]$ denote the greatest integer less than or equal to $t$. Let $f(x)=x-[x]$, $g(x)=1-x+[x]$, and $h(x)=\min\{f(x),g(x)\}$, $x\in[-2,2]$. Then $h$ is:
options: Continuous in $[-2,2]$ but not differentiable at exactly three points in $(-2,2)$
Not continuous at exactly four points in $[-1,2]$
Not continuous at exactly three points in $[-1,2]$
Continuous in $[-2,2]$ but not differentiable at more than four points in $(-2,2)$
questions.key_idea: $h(x)=\min(\{x\},1-\{x\})$ is a continuous zig-zag with a corner at every integer and every half-integer.
solution: $f$ is a rising saw-tooth (slope $1$, jump down at each integer); $g$ is a falling saw-tooth (slope $-1$), with value $1$ at each integer.

Their minimum is the zig-zag with value $0$ at every integer and peaks of height $\frac12$ at every half-integer; the jumps of $f$ and $g$ are never the smaller value, so $h$ has no jump: it is continuous on $[-2,2]$.
Corners of $h$ in $(-2,2)$: at the integers $-1,0,1$ (valleys) and at the half-integers $-\frac32,-\frac12,\frac12,\frac32$ (peaks).
That makes $3+4=7$ points of non-differentiability, which is more than four.
Options (A), (B), (C) fail ((A) says three, (B) and (C) claim discontinuities). Hence (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: $h(x)=\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb{Z})$: a distance function is continuous, and its corners are exactly the points where $\operatorname{dist}$ is $0$ or $\frac12$.
solution: $\min\{\{x\},1-\{x\}\}$ is the distance from $x$ to the nearest integer.
A distance to a closed set is $1$-Lipschitz, hence continuous on $[-2,2]$.
The graph consists of line segments of slope $\pm1$ with direction changes at multiples of $\frac12$, i.e. at $x\in\{-\frac32,-1,-\frac12,0,\frac12,1,\frac32\}$ inside $(-2,2)$.
That is $7$ corners, more than four: option (D) (same answer).

useful_results: On any interval of length $1$ the zig-zag $\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb{Z})$ has two corners (one valley at an integer, one peak at a half-integer).
$x-[x]\in[0,1)$ and $1-x+[x]\in(0,1]$: both lie in $[0,1]$ and add to $1$, so their minimum never exceeds $\frac12$.
Number of corners of the zig-zag in an open interval $(a,b)$ with $a,b$ integers: $2(b-a)-1$ (here $2\cdot4-1=7$).

concepts: Differentiability of the product of a modulus function and a smooth function
questions.question: The function $f(x)=|x^2-2x-3|\cdot e^{|9x^2-12x+4|}$ is not differentiable at exactly:
questions.key_idea: $9x^2-12x+4=(3x-2)^2\ge0$, so the exponential factor is smooth and positive; only the zeros of $x^2-2x-3$ can be corners.
solution: $e^{(3x-2)^2}$ is differentiable and strictly positive for every real $x$.
$|(x-3)(x+1)|$ is non-differentiable only where $(x-3)(x+1)$ changes sign, i.e. at $x=-1$ and $x=3$.
At these points the smooth factor is non-zero: near a simple zero $x_0$ the left and right derivatives of $f$ are $\mp u'(x_0)\,v(x_0)$, which differ since $u'(x_0)\ne0$ and $v(x_0)>0$.
So $f$ is not differentiable at exactly two points, $x=-1$ and $x=3$: option (C).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's working for this question is cut off and garbled: it ends with 'Not differentiable at x = -183' (the points should read $x=-1,\,3$) and never shows why $|9x^2-12x+4|$ can be dropped or why the exponential factor does not matter. Both added; the key (C, two points) is correct. The English option list also labels two options '(C)'; the Hindi list shows (A) one, (B) three, (C) two, (D) four.
useful_results: If $f=|u|\cdot v$ with $v$ differentiable and $v\ne0$, then $f$ is non-differentiable exactly at the zeros of $u$ at which $u'\ne0$ (simple zeros of odd multiplicity).
If $v(x_0)=0$ too, the corner can disappear, e.g. $|x|\cdot x$ is differentiable at $0$; always check the other factor at the zero.
$ax^2+bx+c$ with $b^2=4ac$ is a perfect square, so $|ax^2+bx+c|=ax^2+bx+c$ when $a>0$.

concepts: Continuity at a point
Standard limits: logarithmic and trigonometric ratios
questions.question: If the function $f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac1x\log_e\left(\dfrac{1+\frac xa}{1-\frac xb}\right), & x<0\\ k, & x=0\\ \dfrac{\cos^2x-\sin^2x-1}{\sqrt{x^2+1}-1}, & x>0\end{cases}$ is continuous at $x=0$, then $\dfrac1a+\dfrac1b+\dfrac4k$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Rationalise the right-hand piece to get $-4$; the left-hand piece splits into two standard limits $\frac1a+\frac1b$.
solution: Right limit: multiply by $\frac{\sqrt{x^2+1}+1}{\sqrt{x^2+1}+1}$. Since $\cos^2x-\sin^2x-1=\cos2x-1=-2\sin^2x$, we get $f(0^+)=\lim_{x\to0^+}\frac{-2\sin^2x}{x^2}\left(\sqrt{x^2+1}+1\right)$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF labels the left-hand limit as '$f(0^+)=\frac1a+\frac1b$' (it should be $f(0^-)$, the branch for $x<0$) and has a stray text fragment '$(9\sqrt2,2)$' in the middle of the working; both removed. The value $\frac1a+\frac1b=-4$ and the answer $-5$ are unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Replace each factor by its leading Taylor term: $\sqrt{1+x^2}-1\approx\frac{x^2}{2}$, $\cos2x-1\approx-2x^2$, $\ln(1+u)\approx u$.
solution: $\ln\left(1+\frac xa\right)\approx\frac xa$ and $\ln\left(1-\frac xb\right)\approx-\frac xb$, so $\frac1x\ln\frac{1+x/a}{1-x/b}\approx\frac1a+\frac1b$.

useful_results: $\cos^2x-\sin^2x=\cos2x$, and $1-\cos2x=2\sin^2x$: this converts such quotients to $\frac{\sin^2x}{x^2}$.
$\sqrt{1+u}-1\approx\frac u2$ for small $u$; or rationalise: $\sqrt{1+u}-1=\frac{u}{\sqrt{1+u}+1}$.
$\lim_{x\to0}\frac1x\ln\frac{1+px}{1+qx}=p-q$.

Standard limits: trigonometric ratios
questions.question: Let $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$, $b\ne0$. Define a function $f(x)=\begin{cases}a\sin\dfrac\pi2(x-1), & \text{for } x\le0\\ \dfrac{\tan2x-\sin2x}{bx^3}, & \text{for } x>0\end{cases}$. If $f$ is continuous at $x=0$, then $10-ab$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: $\tan2x-\sin2x=\tan2x(1-\cos2x)\sim2x\cdot2x^2=4x^3$, so the right-hand limit is $\frac4b$.
solution: $f(0)=a\sin\left(-\frac\pi2\right)=-a$, which equals the left-hand limit (sine is continuous).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the Taylor expansion $\tan t-\sin t=\frac{t^3}{2}+O(t^5)$ with $t=2x$.

useful_results: $\tan t-\sin t\sim\frac{t^3}{2}$ as $t\to0$ (so $\frac{\tan t-\sin t}{t^3}\to\frac12$), and $\tan t-\sin t=\tan t(1-\cos t)$.
General: $\tan kx-\sin kx\sim\frac{k^3x^3}{2}$; here $k=2$ gives $4x^3$.
Continuity at a boundary point of a piecewise function with a sine on the left: just evaluate the sine at $x=0$.

concepts: Discontinuity of functions with the greatest integer function
questions.question: Let $[t]$ denote the greatest integer $\le t$. The number of points where the function $f(x)=[x]\,|x^2-1|+\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{[x]+3}\right)-[x+1]$, $x\in(-2,2)$ is not continuous is ______.
questions.key_idea: Only the integers $-1,0,1$ can be points of discontinuity (where $[x]$ jumps); on each interval $[n,n+1)$ the function is a fixed smooth expression.
solution: At $x=-1$: left limit $-2+3=1$, right limit $1$, $f(-1)=1$: continuous.
The function is not continuous at exactly $2$ points ($x=0$ and $x=1$).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's piece list is labelled $(-2,-1]$ for the first piece and $(-1,0)$ for the second, which puts $x=-1$ in the wrong piece ($[-1]=-1$, so $x=-1$ belongs to $[-1,0)$); the value at $-1$ happens to be the same ($1$), so the answer is unaffected. The PDF also lists the pieces without verifying continuity at $x=-1$; that check is added. Final answer $2$ unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Only $[x]$ can jump: compute the jump of $f$ at an integer $n$ in one formula and test it for $n=-1,0,1$.
solution: Write $f=[x]\,c(x)+\sin\frac{\pi}{[x]+3}-1$ with $c(x)=|x^2-1|-1$ continuous. Everything except $[x]$ is continuous, so a discontinuity can occur only at integers $n\in\{-1,0,1\}$.
At an integer $n$, $[x]$ goes from $n-1$ (left) to $n$ (value), so $f(n)-f(n^-)=c(n)+\sin\frac{\pi}{n+3}-\sin\frac{\pi}{n+2}$.

useful_results: If $f$ is built from $[x]$ and continuous functions, it can be discontinuous only at integers; the jump there can cancel (as at $x=-1$ here), so test each integer.
$[x+k]=[x]+k$ for any integer $k$.

concepts: Continuity and differentiability of piecewise functions with the greatest integer function
questions.question: Let $f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\sin(x-[x])}{x-[x]}, & x\in(-2,-1)\\ \max\{2x,\,3[|x|]\}, & |x|<1\\ 1, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$ where $[t]$ denotes the greatest integer $\le t$. If $m$ is the number of points where $f$ is not continuous and $n$ is the number of points where $f$ is not differentiable, then the ordered pair $(m,n)$ is:
questions.key_idea: Reduce $f$ to explicit pieces: on $(-1,1)$ it is $\max(2x,0)$; then only $x=-1,0,1$ need checking.
solution: Doubtful points: $x=-1,\,0,\,1$ (at $x=-2$ the left value is $1$ and $\frac{\sin\{x\}}{\{x\}}\to1$ as $x\to-2^+$, with zero slope on both sides, so it is fine).
At $x=0$: $\text{LHL}=0$, $f(0)=0$, $\text{RHL}=0$: continuous. Slopes: $\text{LHD}=0$, $\text{RHD}=2$: not differentiable at $0$.
At $x=-1$: $\text{LHL}=\lim\frac{\sin\{x\}}{\{x\}}$ with $\{x\}\to1^-$, i.e. $\sin1$; $f(-1)=1$; $\text{RHL}=0$. The three values differ: not continuous.
Not continuous at $x=-1$ and $x=1$: $m=2$. Not differentiable at $x=-1,0,1$: $n=3$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the identity $\max(2x,0)=x+|x|$ on $(-1,1)$, so the only corner inside is $x=0$, and test the two end-joints by comparing three values.
solution: On $(-1,1)$: $f(x)=\max(2x,0)=x+|x|$, which is continuous with a single corner at $x=0$ (slope $0$ to slope $2$).
On $(-2,-1)$ the piece $\frac{\sin u}{u}$, $u=\{x\}\in(0,1)$, is smooth; on $x\ge1$ and $x\le-2$ and at $x=-1$ we have the constant value $1$.
Joint $x=1$: left limit $x+|x|\to2$ but $f(1)=1$ and right limit $1$ - a jump.
Joint $x=-1$: left limit $\frac{\sin u}{u}\to\sin1\approx0.84$, right limit $0$, value $1$ - a jump.
Hence $m=2$ (jumps at $\pm1$) and $n=3$ (corner at $0$ plus the two jumps): $(2,3)$ - same answer.

useful_results: $\max(f,0)=\frac{f+|f|}{2}$: for $f=2x$ this is $x+|x|$.
A discontinuity is never differentiable: count jump points among the non-differentiable points and add the corners separately.
$\frac{\sin u}{u}$ is smooth and tends to $1$ as $u\to0$; as $u\to1^-$ it tends to $\sin1$.

concepts: Differentiability of a composite function
Continuity of piecewise functions
questions.question: Let $f,g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be two real valued functions defined as $f(x)=\begin{cases}-|x+3|, & x<0\\ e^{x}, & x\ge0\end{cases}$ and $g(x)=\begin{cases}x^2+k_1x, & x<0\\ 4x+k_2, & x\ge0\end{cases}$, where $k_1$ and $k_2$ are real constants. If $(g\circ f)$ is differentiable at $x=0$, then $(g\circ f)(-4)+(g\circ f)(4)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $g\circ f$ is differentiable at $0$ only if it is continuous there; match values and one-sided slopes at $x=0$ to get $k_1,k_2$.
solution: $f(x)=x+3$ for $x<-3$; $f(x)=-(x+3)$ for $-3\le x<0$; $f(x)=e^x$ for $x\ge0$. Also $f(x)<0$ for $x<0$, $x\ne-3$, while $f(-3)=0$ and $f(x)\ge1$ for $x\ge0$.
Since $g(u)=u^2+k_1u$ for $u<0$ and $4u+k_2$ for $u\ge0$: for $x<-3$, $(g\circ f)(x)=(x+3)^2+k_1(x+3)$; for $-3<x<0$, $(g\circ f)(x)=(x+3)^2-k_1(x+3)$; for $x\ge0$, $(g\circ f)(x)=4e^x+k_2$.
Continuity at $x=0$ (needed for differentiability): $(g\circ f)(0^-)=9-3k_1$ and $(g\circ f)(0)=4+k_2$, so $9-3k_1=4+k_2$, i.e. $3k_1+k_2=5$.
Differentiate the pieces: $2(x+3)-k_1$ for $-3<x<0$ and $4e^x$ for $x>0$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF puts $x=-3$ in the middle piece $-3\le x<0$ and writes $(x+3)^2-k_1(x+3)$ there, but $f(-3)=0$ so $g(f(-3))=g(0)=k_2$ (a single isolated point). It does not affect differentiability at $0$ or the values at $\pm4$, so $k_1=2$, $k_2=-1$ and the answer are unchanged. I used $-3<x<0$ for that piece.

alternate_solutions.idea: Chain rule at the corner: $f$ is discontinuous at $0$ ($f(0^-)=-3$, $f(0)=1$), so use the left piece of $g$ at the argument $-3$ and the right piece at $1$.
solution: Near $0^-$: $f(x)\to-3$ with $f'(0^-)=-1$ (since $f=-(x+3)$), and $g$ acts through its $x<0$ piece $g_1(u)=u^2+k_1u$.

useful_results: Differentiability of $g\circ f$ at a point where $f$ is discontinuous is possible only if the two one-sided compositions agree in value and slope.
For composites of piecewise functions, first find which piece of the outer function is active, then substitute.
Chain rule one-sidedly: $(g\circ f)'(a^\pm)=g'(f(a^\pm))\cdot f'(a^\pm)$, with the outer piece chosen by the sign of $f(a^\pm)$.

concepts: Continuity and differentiability of a minimum of functions
questions.question: Let $f(x)=\min\{1,\,1+x\sin x\}$, $0\le x\le2\pi$. If $m$ is the number of points where $f$ is not differentiable and $n$ is the number of points where $f$ is not continuous, then the ordered pair $(m,n)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $x\sin x\ge0$ on $[0,\pi]$ and $\le0$ on $[\pi,2\pi]$, so $f=1$ on $[0,\pi]$ and $f=1+x\sin x$ on $[\pi,2\pi]$.
solution: On $[0,\pi]$, $\sin x\ge0$, so $1+x\sin x\ge1$ and $f(x)=1$. On $[\pi,2\pi]$, $\sin x\le0$, so $1+x\sin x\le1$ and $f(x)=1+x\sin x$.
So $f(x)=1$ for $0\le x<\pi$ and $f(x)=1+x\sin x$ for $\pi\le x\le2\pi$.
Continuity: $f(0^+)=1=f(0)$; $f(\pi^-)=1$, $f(\pi)=1+\pi\sin\pi=1$, $f(\pi^+)=1$; $f(2\pi^-)=1$, $f(2\pi)=1$. So $f$ is continuous everywhere and $n=0$.
At $x=\pi$: $f'(\pi^-)=0$ and $f'(\pi^+)=\sin\pi+\pi\cos\pi=-\pi$, so $f$ is not differentiable at $\pi$.
No other interior point is a problem, so $m=1$ and $(m,n)=(1,0)$, option (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $\min\{1,1+u\}=1+\min\{0,u\}=1+\frac{u-|u|}{2}$ with $u=x\sin x$; corners come only from the zeros of $u$ at which $u'\ne0$.
solution: $f(x)=1+\frac{u-|u|}{2}$ with $u=x\sin x$. Since $u$ and $|u|$ are continuous, $f$ is continuous on $[0,2\pi]$: $n=0$.
$|u|$ is non-differentiable exactly at zeros of $u$ where $u'\ne0$. Zeros of $u$ in $[0,2\pi]$: $x=0,\pi,2\pi$ ($x\sin x=0$).
$u'(x)=\sin x+x\cos x$: $u'(\pi)=-\pi\ne0$, so $\pi$ is a corner. The points $0$ and $2\pi$ are end-points of the domain, so they are not counted.

useful_results: $\min(a,b)=\frac{a+b-|a-b|}{2}$ and $\max(a,b)=\frac{a+b+|a-b|}{2}$: a min/max of two differentiable functions has corners only where they cross with unequal slopes.
$f=\min(1,1+u)$ is $1$ when $u\ge0$ and $1+u$ when $u\le0$: the sign pattern of $x\sin x$ on $[0,2\pi]$ is $+$ on $(0,\pi)$ and $-$ on $(\pi,2\pi)$.
Corner test at a crossing $u=0$: slopes are $0$ and $u'$; a corner appears iff $u'\ne0$.

concepts: Continuity of piecewise functions with the greatest integer function
questions.question: Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined as $f(x)=\begin{cases}[e^{x}], & x<0\\ ae^{x}+[x-1], & 0\le x<1\\ b+[\sin(\pi x)], & 1\le x<2\\ [e^{-x}]-c, & x\ge2\end{cases}$ where $a,b,c\in\mathbb{R}$ and $[t]$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $t$. Then, which of the following statements is true?
options: There exist $a,b,c\in\mathbb{R}$ such that $f$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$
If $f$ is discontinuous at exactly one point, then $a+b+c=1$
If $f$ is discontinuous at exactly one point, then $a+b+c\ne1$
$f$ is discontinuous at at least two points, for any values of $a$, $b$ and $c$
questions.key_idea: The constants $a$ and $b+c$ are fixed by the joints $x=0$ and $x=2$; the joint $x=1$ is discontinuous for every $a,b$.
solution: At $x=1$: $f(1)=b$ but $\text{RHL}=b-1$ for every $b$ (and $\text{LHL}=ae-1$). Since $f(1)\ne\text{RHL}$, $f$ is discontinuous at $x=1$ for all values of $a,b,c$.
Hence (A) is false: $f$ is always discontinuous at $x=1$.
If $f$ is discontinuous at exactly one point, that point is $x=1$, so $a=1$ and $b+c=1$, giving $a+b+c=2\ne1$. So (C) is true and (B) is false.
(D) is false: with $a=1$, $b+c=1$, $f$ is discontinuous only at $x=1$. Answer (C).
useful_results: $[\sin\pi x]$ is $-1$ for $x\in(1,2)$, $0$ at integers, $0$ for $x\in(0,1)$ (not $-1$): the sign of the sine decides the floor.
When a statement asks about 'exactly one point of discontinuity', first find the points that are discontinuous for every parameter value, then see which parameters remove the rest.

concepts: Continuity of a composite function
Greatest integer function
questions.question: Let $f,g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be functions defined by $f(x)=\begin{cases}[x], & x<0\\ |1-x|, & x\ge0\end{cases}$ and $g(x)=\begin{cases}e^x-x, & x<0\\ (x-1)^2-1, & x\ge0\end{cases}$ where $[x]$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$. Then, the function $f\circ g$ is discontinuous at exactly:
questions.key_idea: Find which piece of $f$ is active: $g<0$ only for $0<x<2$, where $f(g)=[g]=-1$, while $f(0)=1$ and $f(2)=1$ force jumps at $0$ and $2$.
solution: For $0<x<2$: $g(x)=(x-1)^2-1\in[-1,0)$, so $f(g(x))=[g(x)]=-1$ (a constant), written in the PDF as $[(x-1)^2-1]$.
All other points are continuous (each piece is continuous on its open interval).
So $f\circ g$ is discontinuous at exactly two points ($x=0$ and $x=2$): option (B).
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes the middle piece as '$\left[(x-1)^2-1\right]$' without simplifying it to $-1$ (the value of $[g]$ on $0<x<2$ since $g\in[-1,0)$), and its graph is drawn without a check at $x=2$ against $f(g(2))=1$; the conclusion is right but incomplete. Both added; the answer (two points) is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: $f$ itself is discontinuous only at $0$ (jump from $-1$ to $1$), so $f\circ g$ can be discontinuous only where $g$ passes through $0$.
solution: $g(x)\ge-1$ for all $x$, and on $[-1,\infty)$ the function $f$ is continuous except at $u=0$: $f(u)=[u]=-1$ on $[-1,0)$, $f(u)=|1-u|$ on $[0,\infty)$, with $f(0^-)=-1$ but $f(0)=1$.
So $f\circ g$ can fail to be continuous only where $g(x)=0$, and only if $g$ takes values below $0$ near there (since $g$ is continuous).

At $x=0$: $g$ is positive for $x<0$ but negative just to the right; so the limit values are $f(g\to0^+)=1$ (left) and $f(g\to0^-)=-1$ (right): a jump. At $x=2$: $g<0$ on the left and $>0$ on the right: a jump.
Hence exactly two points - option (B) (same answer).

useful_results: For $f\circ g$, find the points of discontinuity of $f$ (outer) and the values of $x$ where $g$ takes them; then check the approach direction.
If the outer function is discontinuous at $u_0$ and the inner function crosses $u_0$ (or touches it from the discontinuous side), the composite is discontinuous there.

concepts: Discontinuity of functions with the greatest integer function and quadratics
questions.question: The number of points where the function $f(x)=\begin{cases}|2x^2-3x-7|, & \text{if } x\le-1\\ [4x^2-1], & \text{if } -1<x<1\\ |x+1|+|x-2|, & \text{if } x\ge1\end{cases}$, $[t]$ denotes the greatest integer $\le t$, is discontinuous is ______.
questions.key_idea: On $(-1,1)$ the floor of $4x^2-1$ jumps each time $4x^2-1$ crosses the integers $0,1,2$; add the joints $x=\pm1$.
solution: The outer pieces $|2x^2-3x-7|$ and $|x+1|+|x-2|$ are continuous on their own intervals; $f(-1)=|2+3-7|=2$ and $f(1)=|2|+|-1|=3$.
For $x\in(-1,1)$: $4x^2-1\in[-1,3)$. Its floor jumps at every $x$ where $4x^2-1$ passes through an integer value $0$, $1$ or $2$ (it is strictly monotone on each side of $x=0$).
At $x=0$ the quadratic has its minimum $-1$ and $[4x^2-1]=-1$ on both sides, so there is no jump there.

alternate_solutions.idea: On $(-1,1)$ the function is even and $4x^2-1$ is strictly increasing on $(0,1)$ from $-1$ to $3$: count integer crossings on $(0,1)$ once and double.
solution: For $x\in(-1,1)$, $f(-x)=[4x^2-1]=f(x)$: $f$ is even there, so count jumps on $(0,1)$ and mirror them.
On $(0,1)$, $4x^2-1$ increases continuously and strictly from $-1$ to $3$; $[4x^2-1]$ jumps exactly when it passes the integers $0,1,2$ - three jumps (at $x=\frac12,\frac1{\sqrt2},\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$).
Mirror image on $(-1,0)$: three more. At $x=0$ there is no jump (minimum value $-1$ approached from above: floor stays $-1$).

useful_results: The floor of a continuous strictly monotone function jumps once at each integer value it crosses. At a local minimum whose value is an integer $m$ the floor stays $m$ on both sides (no jump); at a local maximum with integer value $m$ the floor is $m-1$ on both sides but $m$ at the point (a removable jump).
Joint check: compare left limit, value and right limit; a discontinuity at the joint can hide behind a floor limit like $[3^-]=2$.
Even function $\Rightarrow$ discontinuities come in symmetric pairs; check $x=0$ separately.

concepts: Discontinuity of a composite function with the greatest integer function
questions.question: Let $f(x)=[2x^2+1]$ and $g(x)=\begin{cases}2x-3, & x<0\\ 2x+3, & x\ge0\end{cases}$, where $[t]$ is the greatest integer $\le t$. Then, in the open interval $(-1,1)$, the number of points where $f\circ g$ is discontinuous is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: $(f\circ g)(x)=[2g(x)^2]+1$ jumps once for every integer value that $2g^2$ passes through, on each side of $0$.
solution: For $x\in(-1,0)$: $g=2x-3\in(-5,-3)$, so $(2x-3)^2\in(9,25)$ and $2(2x-3)^2\in(18,50)$. This is continuous and strictly monotone (decreasing from $50$ to $18$ as $x$ goes from $-1$ to $0$).
Its floor is discontinuous exactly when $2(2x-3)^2\in\{19,20,\dots,49\}$: that is $31$ points.
For $x\in[0,1)$: $g=2x+3\in[3,5)$, so $(2x+3)^2\in[9,25)$ and $2(2x+3)^2\in[18,50)$, strictly increasing from $18$.
Its floor is discontinuous exactly when $2(2x+3)^2\in\{19,20,\dots,49\}$: again $31$ points.
At $x=0$: $2g^2\to18^+$ from both sides (from the left $2(2x-3)^2\to18^+$ and from the right $2(2x+3)^2\to18^+$) and $2g(0)^2=18$, so $f\circ g$ is continuous at $0$ even though $g$ jumps there.
Total number of points of discontinuity $=31+31=62$.
questions.correction_note: In part (ii) the PDF writes the expression as $2(2x-3)^2$; it should be $2(2x+3)^2$ (the branch $g=2x+3$ for $x\ge0$). It also does not check the point $x=0$ where $g$ jumps; that check is added. The count $31+31=62$ is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: $g(x)^2=(2|x|+3)^2$ for every $x$, so $f\circ g$ is an even function of a single increasing quantity in $|x|$: count the jumps for $x\in(0,1)$ and double.
solution: This is an even function of $x$, so discontinuities occur symmetrically about $0$.
For $s=|x|\in(0,1)$, $2(2s+3)^2$ increases strictly and continuously from $18$ to $50$; the floor jumps at each of the $31$ integers $19,\dots,49$.
The point $x=0$: $2(2|x|+3)^2$ has a minimum value $18$ (an integer) at $0$, so the floor is constant $18$ near $0$: no jump.

useful_results: $g(x)^2$ for a two-branch linear $g$ with opposite signs of the constant ($2x-3$ for $x<0$, $2x+3$ for $x\ge0$) equals $(2|x|+3)^2$: spotting this symmetry halves the work.
The floor of a continuous strictly monotone function on an interval is discontinuous at one point for each integer strictly between its end values (here the integers $19,\dots,49$: $31$ of them).
At an end value that is an integer ($18$ here), check whether $\phi$ approaches it from the correct side; if it does, there is no jump.

concepts: Continuity at a point
Standard limits: logarithmic and trigonometric ratios
questions.question: If the function $f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\log_e(1-x+x^2)+\log_e(1+x+x^2)}{\sec x-\cos x}, & x\in\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)-\{0\}\\ k, & x=0\end{cases}$ is continuous at $x=0$, then $k$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The two logarithms combine to $\ln(1+x^2+x^4)$ and $\sec x-\cos x=\frac{\sin^2x}{\cos x}$, so the quotient behaves like $\frac{x^2}{x^2}$.
solution: Write it as $\frac{\ln(1+x^2+x^4)}{x^2+x^4}\cdot x^2(1+x^2)\cdot\cos x\cdot\frac{1}{\left(\frac{\sin x}{x}\right)^2x^2}$.
Each factor tends to: $1$, then $(1+x^2)\to1$, $\cos x\to1$, $\left(\frac{\sin x}{x}\right)^2\to1$ with $x^2$ cancelling. Hence $k=1$, option (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Compare leading terms: $\ln(1+x^2+x^4)\sim x^2$ and $\sec x-\cos x\sim\left(1+\frac{x^2}{2}\right)-\left(1-\frac{x^2}{2}\right)=x^2$.
solution: $\sec x=1+\frac{x^2}{2}+O(x^4)$ and $\cos x=1-\frac{x^2}{2}+O(x^4)$, so $\sec x-\cos x=x^2+O(x^4)$.

useful_results: $\sec x-\cos x=\frac{\sin^2x}{\cos x}=\sin x\tan x\sim x^2$.
$\ln(1+u)\sim u$ as $u\to0$, so the numerator is $\sim x^2$.

concepts: Continuity of piecewise functions
Composite functions
questions.question: If $f(x)=\begin{cases}x+a, & x\le0\\ |x-4|, & x>0\end{cases}$ and $g(x)=\begin{cases}x+1, & x<0\\ (x-4)^2+b, & x\ge0\end{cases}$ are continuous on $\mathbb{R}$, then $(g\circ f)(2)+(f\circ g)(-2)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Continuity at $x=0$ fixes $a=4$ and $b=-15$; then evaluate each composite by pieces.
useful_results: For piecewise functions continuous on $\mathbb{R}$, equate the one-sided limits at each joint; only the joint $x=0$ matters here.
Evaluate composites from the inside out, choosing the piece by the sign condition of the inner value.
$g\circ f$ and $f\circ g$ are in general different functions: do not swap the order.

concepts: Continuity at a point
Standard limits: binomial expansion for fractional powers
questions.question: If for $p\ne q\ne0$, the function $f(x)=\dfrac{\sqrt[7]{p(729+x)}-3}{\sqrt[3]{729+qx}-9}$ is continuous at $x=0$, then:
questions.key_idea: The denominator $\to0$, so the numerator must vanish: $p\cdot3^6=3^7$ gives $p=3$; then factor out $(1+\frac{x}{729})^{1/7}-1$ and $(1+\frac{qx}{729})^{1/3}-1$.
solution: $f(0)=\lim_{x\to0}f(x)$, and this limit must be of the $\frac00$ form (the denominator tends to $\sqrt[3]{729}-9=0$).
So the numerator must tend to $0$: $\sqrt[7]{p\cdot729}-3=0\Rightarrow p\cdot3^6=3^7\Rightarrow p=3$.
Use $(1+u)^{m}-1\sim mu$: the numerator $\sim3\cdot\frac17\cdot\frac{x}{3^6}$ and the denominator $\sim9\cdot\frac13\cdot\frac{qx}{3^6}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Differentiate: with $N(x)=\sqrt[7]{p(729+x)}-3$ and $D(x)=\sqrt[3]{729+qx}-9$ both $\to0$, $f(0)=\frac{N'(0)}{D'(0)}$ (L'Hopital).

useful_results: Binomial linearisation: $(1+u)^m-1\sim mu$ as $u\to0$, for any real $m$.
$0/0$ forms: when $N(a)=D(a)=0$ and both are differentiable with $D'(a)\ne0$, $\lim\frac{N}{D}=\frac{N'(a)}{D'(a)}$.
To keep a limit finite at a root of the denominator, the numerator's parameter is forced (here $p=3$).

concepts: Limit of a sequence-defined function (powers of $x$)
Continuity of a function defined by a limit
questions.question: The function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ defined by $f(x)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\dfrac{\cos(2\pi x)-x^{2n}\sin(x-1)}{1+x^{2n+1}-x^{2n}}$ is continuous for all $x$ in:
questions.key_idea: Treat $|x|<1$, $|x|>1$ and $x=\pm1$ separately (the limit of $x^{2n}$ is $0,\infty,1$); then compare left limit, value and right limit at $\pm1$.
solution: For $|x|>1$: divide numerator and denominator by $x^{2n}$: $f(x)=\lim\frac{\frac{\cos2\pi x}{x^{2n}}-\sin(x-1)}{\frac{1}{x^{2n}}+x-1}=-\frac{\sin(x-1)}{x-1}$.
At $x=-1$: $\text{RHL}=\cos(-2\pi)=1$, $\text{LHL}=-\frac{\sin(-2)}{-2}=-\frac{\sin2}{2}$ and $f(-1)=-(1+\sin2)$: all three differ, not continuous.
For other $x$ the expression is a continuous function on each of $|x|<1$ and $|x|>1$. So $f$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}-\{-1,1\}$, option (B).
useful_results: $\lim_{n\to\infty}x^{2n}=0$ for $|x|<1$, $=1$ for $|x|=1$, $=\infty$ for $|x|>1$; $x^{2n+1}$ behaves like $x\cdot x^{2n}$ (and equals $-1$ at $x=-1$).
For ratios of expressions in $x^{2n}$: divide by the largest power for $|x|>1$, and substitute directly for $|x|<1$ and $x=\pm1$.
The function defined by such a limit is continuous on each region and its only possible discontinuities are the boundary points $|x|=1$.

concepts: Differentiability of functions involving modulus
questions.question: The number of points, where the function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, $f(x)=|x-1|\cos|x-2|\sin|x-1|+(x-3)|x^2-5x+4|$ is NOT differentiable, is:
questions.key_idea: $|t|\sin|t|=t\sin t$ and $\cos|t|=\cos t$ are smooth; only $(x-3)|(x-1)(x-4)|$ has corners, at $x=1$ and $x=4$.
solution: PDF's form: $f(x)=|x-1|\left[\cos|x-2|\sin|x-1|+(x-3)|x-4|\right]$ - the candidates for non-differentiability are $x=1,2,4$ (zeros of the modulus arguments).

First term: $|x-1|\sin|x-1|=(x-1)\sin(x-1)$ (the function $t\sin t$ is even, so $|t|\sin|t|=t\sin t$) and $\cos|x-2|=\cos(x-2)$ (cosine is even). So $T_1=(x-1)\sin(x-1)\cos(x-2)$ is differentiable everywhere; in particular $x=2$ is not a problem.
Second term: $T_2=(x-3)\,|(x-1)(x-4)|$. The modulus is non-differentiable exactly at its simple zeros $x=1$ and $x=4$.
At these points the smooth factor $(x-3)$ is non-zero: $-2$ at $x=1$ and $1$ at $x=4$. So $T_2$ has a corner at each of $x=1$ and $x=4$.
A differentiable function plus a function with a corner has a corner: $f$ is not differentiable at $x=1$ and $x=4$.
Hence the number of points is $2$, option (B).
questions.correction_note: The PDF factors out $|x-1|$ and concludes 'non-differentiable at $x=1$ and $x=4$' without justification; the bracket still contains $\sin|x-1|$ and $|x-4|$, which are themselves non-differentiable, so the factorisation alone proves nothing (and it never explains why $x=2$, where $\cos|x-2|$ has a modulus, is not a point). The justification above (even-function identities for the first term, simple-zero rule for the second) replaces it; the conclusion (2 points) is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Near each candidate point write $f$ as a smooth function plus $c\,|x-a|$ and compute the corner coefficient $c$ (products of two vanishing moduli are second-order small and never give a corner).
solution: Candidates: $x=1,2,4$. At $x=2$: $\cos|x-2|=\cos(x-2)$ is smooth, so no corner.
Near $x=1$: $|x-1|\cos|x-2|\sin|x-1|\approx|x-1|\cdot\cos1\cdot|x-1|=\cos1\,(x-1)^2$, which has zero slope on both sides - no corner from $T_1$.
Near $x=1$: $(x-3)\,|(x-1)(x-4)|\approx(-2)\cdot3|x-1|=-6|x-1|$ - a corner with slope jump $-12\ne0$.
Near $x=4$: $T_1$ is smooth, and $(x-3)|(x-1)(x-4)|\approx1\cdot3|x-4|$ - a corner (slope jump $6\ne0$).
Corners at exactly $x=1$ and $x=4$: $2$ points (same answer).

useful_results: $|t|\sin|t|=t\sin t$ and $\cos|t|=\cos t$: odd/even functions of $|t|$ lose their modulus. In general $\phi(|t|)$ is smooth at $0$ iff $\phi'(0)=0$ (for $\phi$ differentiable).
$g(x)\,|(x-a)|$ is non-differentiable at $a$ iff $g(a)\ne0$ (a simple zero of the modulus argument); $|x-a|^k$ with $k\ge2$ is differentiable at $a$.
A sum $S+C$ with $S$ differentiable and $C$ having a corner at $a$ has a corner at $a$.

concepts: Continuity at a point
Standard limits: logarithmic
questions.question: Let the function $f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\log_e(1+5x)-\log_e(1+\alpha x)}{x}, & \text{if } x\ne0\\ 10, & \text{if } x=0\end{cases}$ be continuous at $x=0$. Then $\alpha$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Each logarithm gives a limit $\frac{\ln(1+kx)}{x}\to k$, so the limit is $5-\alpha$.
solution: Use the expansion $\ln(1+u)=u-\frac{u^2}{2}+\dots$ for $u=5x$ and $u=\alpha x$: the numerator is $(5x-\dots)-(\alpha x-\dots)$.
Divide by $x$: the quotient is $(5-\alpha)+(\text{terms in }x)\to5-\alpha$ as $x\to0$.
So the limit is $5-\alpha$, and continuity requires $5-\alpha=10$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The limit is the derivative at $0$ of $h(x)=\ln(1+5x)-\ln(1+\alpha x)$, because $h(0)=0$.

useful_results: $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\ln(1+px)-\ln(1+qx)}{x}=p-q$ (the derivative of $\ln\frac{1+px}{1+qx}$ at $0$).
$\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\ln(1+kx)}{x}=k$, $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^{kx}-1}{x}=k$.
A limit of the form $\frac{h(x)-h(0)}{x}$ is simply $h'(0)$.

concepts: Continuity and differentiability of piecewise functions with the greatest integer function
Quadratic inequalities
questions.question: Let $f(x)=\begin{cases}|4x^2-8x+5|, & \text{if } 8x^2-6x+1\ge0\\ [4x^2-8x+5], & \text{if } 8x^2-6x+1<0\end{cases}$ where $[\alpha]$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $\alpha$. Then the number of points in $\mathbb{R}$ where $f$ is not differentiable is ______.
questions.key_idea: On $(\frac14,\frac12)$ the function is the floor of a strictly decreasing quadratic (a staircase), outside it equals the quadratic itself; check the two ends and the step.
solution: On $(-\infty,1)$, $h$ is strictly decreasing: $h\left(\frac14\right)=\frac{13}{4}$ and $h\left(\frac12\right)=2$. So for $x\in(\frac14,\frac12)$, $h(x)\in(2,\frac{13}{4})$.
$h(x)=3\iff4x^2-8x+2=0\iff x=\frac{2-\sqrt2}{2}\approx0.293$ (the other root exceeds $1$), which lies in $(\frac14,\frac12)$.
At $x=\frac14$: $f\left(\frac14\right)=h\left(\frac14\right)=\frac{13}{4}$ while $f\left(\frac14^+\right)=3$: discontinuous, hence not differentiable.
At $x=\frac{2-\sqrt2}{2}$: $f$ drops from $3$ to $2$: discontinuous, hence not differentiable.

At $x=\frac12$: $f\left(\frac12\right)=h\left(\frac12\right)=2$ equals the left limit $2$, so $f$ is continuous, but $f'\left(\frac12^-\right)=0$ and $f'\left(\frac12^+\right)=h'\left(\frac12\right)=8\cdot\frac12-8=-4$: not differentiable.
Elsewhere $f$ is a polynomial or a constant. Hence $f$ is not differentiable at exactly $3$ points ($x=\frac14,\frac{2-\sqrt2}{2},\frac12$).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's piecewise list gives '$3$ on $\left(\frac14,\frac{2-\sqrt2}{2}\right)$ and $2$ on $\left[\frac{2-\sqrt2}{2},\frac12\right)$'. At $x_0=\frac{2-\sqrt2}{2}$ we have $h(x_0)=3$ exactly, so $f(x_0)=[3]=3$: the point belongs to the first piece ($3$ on $\left(\frac14,x_0\right]$, $2$ on $\left(x_0,\frac12\right)$). The set of three bad points and the answer are unchanged. I also added the explicit value $h\left(\frac14\right)=\frac{13}{4}$ which explains the jump at $x=\frac14$ (the PDF only shows the graph).
useful_results: $f=\begin{cases}A & \text{if } P\ge0\\ B & \text{if } P<0\end{cases}$: the joints are the roots of $P$; at each joint compare $A$'s and $B$'s values and slopes.
The floor of a strictly monotone function is a staircase: its jump points are where the function equals an integer; a jump point whose value sits exactly on the integer belongs to the upper step.
Quadratic $4(x-1)^2+1$: strictly decreasing for $x<1$, minimum value $1$ at $x=1$.

concepts: Differentiability of functions with the greatest integer function and modulus
questions.question: If $[t]$ denotes the greatest integer $\le t$, then the number of points at which the function $f(x)=4|2x+3|+9\left[x+\frac12\right]-12[x+20]$ is not differentiable in the open interval $(-20,20)$, is ______.
questions.key_idea: $[x]$ jumps at integers and $[x+\frac12]$ jumps at half-integers: every such point is a non-differentiability point; the corner of $|2x+3|$ at $-\frac32$ lies on one of them.
solution: The three sources of non-differentiability are: $|2x+3|$ (corner at $x=-\frac32$), $[x]$ (jumps at integers) and $\left[x+\frac12\right]$ (jumps at half-integers $k+\frac12$).
At every integer $n\in(-20,20)$, $[x]$ jumps by $1$ and the other terms are continuous, so $f$ jumps by $-12$: not differentiable. Integers $-19,\dots,19$: $39$ points.

At every half-integer $k+\frac12\in(-20,20)$, $\left[x+\frac12\right]$ jumps by $1$ while the other terms are continuous, so $f$ jumps by $9$: not differentiable. These are $-19.5,-18.5,\dots,19.5$: $40$ points.
The corner of $|2x+3|$ at $x=-\frac32$ is itself a half-integer (already counted: $f$ is discontinuous there), so it adds nothing new.
questions.correction_note: The PDF counts $39$ points $x=I+\frac12$ with $I\in\{-19,\dots,19\}$ (that list misses $x=-19.5$; there are $40$ half-integers in $(-20,20)$) and then adds $x=-\frac32$ as a separate extra point ($39+39+1$), although $-\frac32$ is already one of the half-integers. The two slips cancel, so the printed total $79$ is correct; the corrected count is $39+40=79$.

alternate_solutions.idea: All jumps occur where $2x$ is an integer: even values of $2x$ give the jumps of $[x]$, odd values give those of $[x+\frac12]$, so count the integers $2x\in(-40,40)$.
solution: $[x]$ jumps when $x\in\mathbb{Z}$, i.e. $2x$ is even; $\left[x+\frac12\right]$ jumps when $x\in\mathbb{Z}+\frac12$, i.e. $2x$ is odd.
So $f$ has a jump (hence is not differentiable) at $x$ exactly when $2x$ is an integer, i.e. $x\in\frac12\mathbb{Z}$.
The corner of $|2x+3|$ at $x=-\frac32$ ($2x=-3$) is among them, so nothing is added.

useful_results: $[x+\tfrac12]$ is 'round half up'; $[x]$ and $[x+\tfrac12]$ together change at every multiple of $\frac12$, i.e. whenever $[2x]$ changes.
$[x+k]=[x]+k$ for integer $k$ (so the $20$ in $[x+20]$ is just a constant).
In $(-N,N)$ the multiples of $\frac12$ correspond to the integers $2x\in(-2N,2N)$: $4N-1$ of them (here $79$ for $N=20$); always check for double-counting between different sources.
